prompt: On AKS, which of these runs on machines Microsoft operates rather than in your subscription?
hint: The half the tier pays for.

choices.text: kube-proxy, one pod on every node
choices.why: It runs on your nodes, beside your pods, like the DaemonSets kind showed on every worker.

choices.text: The scale set behind the system pool
choices.why: It is in the node resource group of your subscription, billed as virtual machines.

choices.text: CoreDNS, which the system pool exists for
choices.why: CoreDNS is a system pod, and system pods run on your system pool, on your machines.

choices.text: etcd
choices.why: Right. etcd, the API server, the scheduler and the controllers are the control plane, and none of them is on a node you can list.

prompt: What does a cluster on the Free tier lack, compared with one on Standard?
hint: Every AKS feature is on every tier.

choices.text: A financially backed uptime SLA for the API server
choices.why: Right. Free has every feature and a best-effort control plane, with no money behind the promise.

choices.text: Availability zones for its node pools
choices.why: Zones are a property of the pools, and the tier does not decide them.

choices.text: Node pools in user mode
choices.why: A user pool exists on every tier; the mode is not something the tier sells.

choices.text: More than 10 nodes
choices.why: Ten is the recommended ceiling; the documented limit on Free is 1,000 nodes.

prompt: A Standard cluster with availability zones has an uptime SLA of 99.95% on its API server. Over a month of 730 hours, how many minutes may the API server be unreachable without the promise being broken?
hint: 0.05% of 730 hours, in minutes.

prompt: Which of these can the kind cluster of this lesson NOT reproduce? Choose all that apply.
hint: kind is the Kubernetes AKS runs, and nothing Microsoft adds.

choices.text: A node pool as one object with a scale set behind it
choices.why: kind starts Docker containers; nothing groups them into a pool that can be resized or upgraded as one.

choices.text: A drain refused by a PodDisruptionBudget
choices.why: That is Kubernetes, and the lab ran it: the API server refused the evictions the budget did not allow.

choices.text: The orchestration of a surge upgrade
choices.why: Adding the surge node and reimaging the old one are AKS's; the lab stood a cordoned node in for the surge node.

choices.text: A node with the CriticalAddonsOnly taint
choices.why: A taint is a field on a node object, and kubectl put it on shop-worker.

choices.text: A maintenance configuration
choices.why: There is no AKS resource provider in the lab to read one; the Bicep compiler checked its shape and nothing ran it.

prompt: A Standard cluster has all its nodes in zone 1. Zone 1 fails for an hour, every pod is down, and the API server keeps answering. What did the uptime SLA promise here?
hint: Read what the SLA is about.

choices.text: Nothing was broken, because the shop's pods count as part of the control plane
choices.why: Pods are workloads on your nodes; the SLA does not count them at all.

choices.text: That Microsoft moves the nodes to another zone within the hour
choices.why: Nothing in the SLA moves nodes; spreading them over zones is declared on the pool.

choices.text: Only the control plane being reachable, which held, so it was kept
choices.why: Right. The SLA is about the API server and nothing else, and the nodes' zones are your decision.

choices.text: A credit for the hour, since the cluster was down
choices.why: The cluster's API server was up. What was down was yours to spread.

prompt: What keeps the shop's pods off the system pool of an AKS cluster?
hint: A preference is not a refusal.

choices.text: The label kubernetes.azure.com/mode=system on its nodes
choices.why: AKS prefers system pods there because of it, and it refuses nothing to anybody.

choices.text: The taint CriticalAddonsOnly=true:NoSchedule
choices.why: Right. Only pods that tolerate it are scheduled there, and the system pods do while the shop does not.

choices.text: The pool's mode, which AKS checks against each pod's namespace
choices.why: The mode is a property of the pool and nothing compares it with a namespace.

choices.text: Its VM size, which is too small for user workloads
choices.why: A system pool is at least 4 vCPUs and 4 GB, which is room enough for the shop.

prompt: Match each thing written on a node to what it says.
hint: Two labels AKS writes, one taint, and one that only kind has.

pairs.right: The name of the pool the node belongs to
Whether the pool is a system or a user pool
Only pods that tolerate it are scheduled here
kind's control-plane node, which AKS never shows you

right_distractors: The virtual machine size of the node

prompt: The system pods tolerate the taint ___=true:NoSchedule, which is why a dedicated system pool still runs them and nothing else.
hint: Its name says who it is for.

prompt: A team wants Spot capacity for the shop's nightly sales report. Where can it go?
hint: Lesson 5's evictions, and the system pool's restrictions.

choices.text: In the system pool, set to Spot, to save on the nodes that are always on
choices.why: A system pool cannot run on Spot; an eviction there would take CoreDNS with it.

choices.text: In any pool, since Spot is chosen per pod
choices.why: Spot is a property of the scale set behind a pool, so every node in it is Spot or none is.

choices.text: Nowhere: AKS clusters cannot use Spot
choices.why: They can, in user pools.

choices.text: In a user pool of its own, with scaleSetPriority set to Spot
choices.why: Right. Spot pools must be user pools, and a pool of its own keeps the shop's API on regular capacity.

prompt: slip.bicep had a pool named shop-apps, mode: 'system' and maxPods: 300, and the compiler printed one warning, for the name. What does its silence about the other two tell you?
hint: What does a type that admits any string say about a string?

choices.text: Nothing: the documented maximum of 250 pods, and whether system is accepted for System, are the service's to decide
choices.why: Right. Silence is no verdict, and the documentation is where the 250 is written.

choices.text: That both are valid, since the compiler checks against Azure's own types
choices.why: It checks against the types, and these types admit any string for the mode and set no ceiling on maxPods.

choices.text: That Azure will lower maxPods to 250 and capitalise the mode on its own
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so, and a laptop cannot find out what the service would do.

choices.text: That the name warning stopped the compiler before it read the rest
choices.why: A warning stops nothing; the template was written, and a missing check is not a skipped one.

prompt: Put the steps AKS takes to upgrade one node pool with surge in order.
hint: Capacity first, removal last.
items: Add the surge nodes maxSurge asks for
Cordon and drain an old node, as the disruption budgets allow
Reimage the drained node at the new version
Remove the surge nodes once every node is upgraded
trap: The surge node comes first: it is what gives the evicted pods somewhere to go.

prompt: A pool of 10 nodes has maxSurge set to 33%. How many surge nodes does AKS add at a time?
hint: A percentage of the node count, rounded up.

prompt: In the lab, drain asked for all three shop pods at once and two were refused with "would violate the pod's disruption budget". Why did all three end up evicted anyway?
hint: What changed between one retry and the next?

choices.text: drain overrode the budget after its third refusal
choices.why: drain never overrides a budget; it asks again every five seconds until it is allowed or its timeout runs out.

choices.text: Uncordoning shop-worker3 raised minAvailable for the duration of the drain
choices.why: Uncordoning changes where pods may go, and nothing in the budget.

choices.text: Every retry waited until a replacement was ready on the other node
choices.why: Right. Three ready pods with two required allows one at a time, so the evictions were paced by the replacements.

choices.text: The readiness probe failed, so the pods no longer counted
choices.why: A pod that is not ready counts against the budget, not for it; the probes passed throughout.

prompt: A cluster outside long-term support runs 1.35 and has to reach 1.37. How does it get there?
hint: Minor versions, and skipping.

choices.text: In one upgrade, since both versions are inside N-2
choices.why: Being supported does not make a jump allowed; outside LTS no minor version may be skipped.

choices.text: By upgrading the node pools to 1.37 first, then the control plane
choices.why: Pools follow the control plane and may lag it; they never lead it.

choices.text: Only by creating a new cluster on 1.37
choices.why: An upgrade in place works, one minor version at a time.

choices.text: In two upgrades, to 1.36 and then to 1.37
choices.why: Right. One minor version at a time, control plane first each time.

prompt: During an AKS upgrade, a budget of three of three blocks the drain of one node of the pool apps, which has undrainableNodeBehavior: Cordon. What happens? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read what aks.bicep chose, and what a platform-initiated upgrade does.

choices.text: AKS lowers the budget to two of three and drains the node
choices.why: AKS never edits your budget; only a forced or platform-initiated upgrade passes over it.

choices.text: The node is left cordoned and labelled kubernetes.azure.com/upgrade-status=Quarantined
choices.why: That is what Cordon does with a node it cannot drain.

choices.text: The whole upgrade is rolled back to the previous version
choices.why: Nothing rolls back on its own, and a control plane upgrade cannot be rolled back at all.

choices.text: The rest of the pool carries on being upgraded
choices.why: Quarantining one node is what lets the others continue.

choices.text: The blocked node stays on the old version until somebody deals with it
choices.why: The quarantined node is yours to resolve: fix the budget, then the node.

prompt: A pool on Azure CNI has 10 nodes, maxSurge of 1 and maxPods of 30. Microsoft gives the addresses an upgrade needs as (nodes + maxSurge) × (1 + maxPods). How many addresses must the subnet have free for this pool?
hint: One address per node, and one per pod it may run.

prompt: A cluster runs 1.36.2 with upgradeChannel set to stable. Available are 1.35.9, 1.36.6, 1.37.1 and 1.37.3, and 1.37 is the newest minor. What does the channel move it to?
hint: stable is the latest patch of N-1.

choices.why: That is the latest patch of N, which is where rapid goes.
Right. N is 1.37, so N-1 is 1.36, and its latest patch is 1.36.6.
stable does not take the first patch of a newer minor; it stays one minor behind the newest.

choices.text: Nowhere, since 1.36 is already supported
choices.why: stable moves the patch too: 1.36.2 is behind 1.36.6.

prompt: A window has startTime 02:00 and utcOffset -03:00. At what hour does it start in UTC? Answer with the hour only.
hint: Local time minus the offset.

prompt: Match each maintenance configuration to what it schedules.
hint: Two follow a channel; one follows AKS's own releases.

pairs.right: AKS's weekly releases of control plane components and system add-ons
The Kubernetes upgrades the upgradeChannel decides on
The node images the nodeOSUpgradeChannel decides on

right_distractors: Azure's platform maintenance on the hosts under the scale sets

prompt: A window runs from 08:00 to 12:00. A node pool upgrade starts at 11:50 and is still running at 12:15. What does AKS do?
hint: The window bounds one end of the work.

choices.text: Lets it run to the end, and begins nothing new after noon
choices.why: Right. A window bounds when work starts, not when it ends.

choices.text: Stops the upgrade at 12:00 and resumes it in the next window
choices.why: Work in flight is not stopped at the end of a window.

choices.text: Rolls the pool back, since it ran outside the window
choices.why: Nothing rolls back for running late.

choices.text: Lets it finish and then upgrades the next pool straight away
choices.why: Once the window has closed, nothing new starts until the next one.

prompt: A cluster has an aksManagedAutoUpgradeSchedule window every Sunday and upgradeChannel set to none. What happens on Sunday?
hint: A window says when, not what.

choices.text: AKS upgrades it to the latest patch, since a window enables patching
choices.why: Enabling planned maintenance does not enable automatic upgrades.

choices.text: AKS refuses the window, because none and a window cannot coexist
choices.why: Both are accepted; they simply do nothing together.

choices.text: Nothing upgrades its Kubernetes version, because no channel asks for one
choices.why: Right. The window is an appointment, and with none nobody keeps it.

choices.text: The window moves the cluster to stable on its own
choices.why: A window never changes the channel.

prompt: Which of these slips did the Bicep compiler warn about in this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ranges and patterns are in the types; enumerations of strings often are not.

choices.text: durationHours: 2 in a maintenance window
choices.why: The type has a minimum of 4.

choices.text: utcOffset: '-3:00'
choices.why: The type carries the pattern of a sign and two digits each side of the colon.

choices.text: dayOfWeek: 'Sun'
choices.why: It passed: the type of dayOfWeek is any string, and the seven names are the service's rule.

choices.text: nodeSoakDurationInMinutes: 45
choices.why: The type's maximum is 30.

choices.text: drainTimeoutInMinutes: 2
choices.why: It passed: the type allows 1 to 1,440, and the documented minimum of 5 is the service's.

prompt: The pool apps has three nodes, each nearly full, maxSurge 0 and maxUnavailable 1, and the shop has three replicas with minAvailable: 2. What is most likely to stall its upgrade?
hint: No surge means the room comes from the nodes that are left.

choices.text: The system pool's taint, which none of the shop's pods tolerate
choices.why: The taint keeps the shop off the system pool, which was never where its pods could go.

choices.text: maxUnavailable, which a user pool is not allowed to use at all
choices.why: It is the system pool that cannot use maxUnavailable.

choices.text: The soak duration, which defaults to thirty minutes for each node
choices.why: The default soak is 0; 30 is its maximum.

choices.text: Replacements stuck Pending, so the budget allows nothing more
choices.why: Right. Without a surge node the evicted pods need room on two full nodes, and until they are ready the budget refuses the next eviction.

prompt: A cluster outside long-term support is on 1.34 and has to reach 1.37. How many control plane upgrades does that take?
hint: One per minor version.

prompt: kubectl ___ marks a node unschedulable and moves none of its pods; drain does that first, and then evicts them.
hint: The first half of a drain.
